Anxiolytics and Sedative-Hypnotics

benzodiazepines · Z-drugs · ramelteon · orexin antagonists · buspirone · hydroxyzineWhich sedative fits, and what is the risk?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Drug script
Bottom line
  • A benzodiazepine plus alcohol or an opioid can bring respiratory depression and hypotension; alone, breathing is usually only mildly slowed
  • Short half-life (alprazolam): rebound anxiety, harsher withdrawal, more addiction. Liver disease or old age: lorazepam, oxazepam or temazepam
  • Buspirone and ramelteon carry no dependence; suvorexant is contraindicated in narcolepsy
What it is

Benzodiazepines and the Z-drugs (zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone) bind the benzodiazepine site of the gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA-A) receptor

Other mechanisms: buspirone (serotonin 1A partial agonist), ramelteon (melatonin agonist), suvorexant (orexin antagonist), hydroxyzine (first-generation antihistamine)

Mechanism

GABA-A channel opens more often more chloride conductance sedation, anxiolysis, seizure control, dose-dependent anterograde amnesia

Long use downregulates GABA-A receptors tolerance withdrawal after an abrupt stop

Half-life

Short: midazolam, triazolam. Intermediate: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam. Long: diazepam, chlordiazepoxide Half-life tables differThe AnKing half-life table lists both as intermediate; the NBME treats alprazolam as short-acting and clonazepam as the long-acting switch

Shorter half-life: higher addiction potential and more severe withdrawal ATOMATOM may help recall the more addictive group: alprazolam, triazolam, oxazepam, midazolam (alprazolam and oxazepam listed as intermediate in some half-life tables)

Used for

Benzodiazepines: acute anxiety, a bridge while an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) takes effect, alcohol withdrawal, status epilepticus, catatonia (first line)

Z-drugs, ramelteon, suvorexant: insomnia, after cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), at the lowest dose for the shortest time

Buspirone: generalized anxiety disorder when an SSRI or SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) falls short; hydroxyzine: a short-term add-on

Risks

Ongoing use raises the risk of falls (hip fractures may follow), cognitive impairment and car crashes, worst in older adults

Tolerance and withdrawal under supervised prescription are physiologic dependence, not a use disorder

Insights

Glucuronidation alone spares lorazepam, oxazepam and temazepam: it holds up in older age and liver disease; most others need the oxidative step first LOTLOT may help recall them: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam, safe in liver disease

Fast off means rebound: a short half-life brings sympathetic hyperarousal between doses, and a switch to long-acting clonazepam smooths it

2Urgent risks
Respiratory depressionA benzodiazepine or Z-drug taken with alcohol, an opioid or another central nervous system depressant

If breathing slows or blood pressure falls, choose airway, breathing and circulation support; naloxone if an opioid may be involved.

Abrupt stopDaily use stopped suddenly: withdrawal that can be life-threatening, seizures included
ReversalFlumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and Z-drugs but can precipitate withdrawal and seizures in a tolerant user
DisinhibitionA teenager taking a parent's benzodiazepine: disinhibition raises acute suicide risk
3Differential
Which effect is it, most tempting first
EffectFingerprintDecides it
Rebound anxietyAnxiety and sympathetic arousal between dosesShort half-life (alprazolam); a long-acting agent such as clonazepam lowers it
An older adult or child may turn confused and aggressiveTypically within an hour of a dose; a higher dose only worsens it
Nervousness, tremor and seizures after an abrupt stopTiming follows half-life: the shorter it is, the sooner and harsher
Stupor with slow breathing or low blood pressureAbnormal vital signs or pinpoint pupils: a benzodiazepine alone usually keeps vitals near normal and pupils normal
Inner restlessnessAn antipsychotic causes it; a benzodiazepine may treat it
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Agranulocytosis, orthostatic hypotension or urinary retention among the answer choicesClozapine, alpha-1 blockade, anticholinergic drugsNone is a benzodiazepine effect: look for rebound or dependence
Narcolepsy on the problem listOrexin already deficientNo suvorexant
An opioid or nightly alcohol on the historyAdditive respiratory depressionAvoid adding a Z-drug; a benzodiazepine adds the same risk
Active substance use disorderAddiction and dependence riskNo benzodiazepine
Wakes at night and cannot return to sleepNeeds a hypnotic that lasts the nightZolpidem or eszopiclone; not zaleplon or ramelteon
Pause point
Alprazolam just started for panic attacks: what to watch for at follow-up Offered: agranulocytosis, akathisia or orthostatic hypotension A short half-life; no marrow, dopamine-blocking or alpha-1 effect → Rebound anxiety and withdrawal; a long-acting agent such as clonazepam lowers both
Insomnia in a patient with narcolepsy Offered: suvorexant Narcolepsy is an orexin deficiency; an orexin antagonist deepens it → Contraindicated: choose another hypnotic
7Treatment
1

ReboundShort-acting agent, anxiety between doses

Switch to a long-acting benzodiazepine such as clonazepam
2

Liver or ageCirrhosis or older age, and a benzodiazepine is still needed

Lorazepam, oxazepam or temazepam

Not diazepam or chlordiazepoxide: long-acting, avoided when the liver is compromised

3

InsomniaSevere or unresponsive after CBT-I

Lowest dose, shortest course of a rapid-onset, short half-life hypnotic

Older adult: ramelteon; no antihistamine

4

No dependence wantedGeneralized anxiety, second line after an SSRI or SNRI

Buspirone may be considered, alone or as an add-on

No sedation, tolerance, addiction or alcohol interaction In practiceIn practice: the Merck Manual notes that with this drug, symptoms typically ease only once the dose is raised to the upper range

5

Severe symptomsWhile an SSRI or SNRI is being raised

Short-term hydroxyzine or a benzodiazepine as an add-on
6

Long-term useNightly or daily use for weeks

Not indefinitely in most cases, and not stopped abruptly after daily use

8Follow-up
Prescribing a sedative safely
WhenCheckWhy
Before startingAlcohol, opioid and other sedative useAdditive respiratory depression and hypotension
Substance use disorderAvoid benzodiazepinesAddiction and dependence
Older adultAvoid most benzodiazepines; ramelteon for sleep onsetFalls, confusion, slower metabolism
Suvorexant plannedLiver disease, a strong cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) inhibitor, narcolepsyNot recommended or contraindicated
Driving or skilled workCoordination and daytime sleepinessCar crashes with ongoing use
Every visit on long-term useTolerance, dose creep, the need to continueDependence builds; benzodiazepines blunt learning in therapy
Stopping after daily useA taper, never an abrupt stopWithdrawal seizures
Practice
  1. 26-year-old woman seen 1 day after her second emergency visit this month sudden pounding heart, breathlessness and fear of dying, peaking within minutes examination, electrocardiogram and thyroid tests normal; alprazolam started follow-up in 2 weeks → Rebound anxiety → alprazolam's short half-life brings rebound anxiety and withdrawal symptoms, and a long-acting agent such as clonazepam lowers that risk; agranulocytosis belongs to clozapine and urinary retention to anticholinergic drugs
  2. 58-year-old man with cirrhosis admitted for a variceal bleed, now banded and stable severe anxiety and insomnia since admission; no alcohol for 3 months oriented; no tremor or sweating; no asterixis BP 118/72 mm Hg · HR 84/min → Lorazepam → lorazepam, like oxazepam and temazepam, undergoes only glucuronidation, which liver disease spares; long-acting chlordiazepoxide and diazepam are avoided when the liver is compromised
  3. 71-year-old man on long-term oxycodone for spinal stenosis trouble falling asleep for 3 weeks since his wife entered a nursing home drinks 2 glasses of wine nightly; lives alone RR 14/min · oxygen saturation 96% → Alprazolam → a benzodiazepine taken with an opioid or alcohol can bring respiratory depression and hypotension, and in older adults it adds confusion and falls; cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia comes first, and ramelteon is safe in older adults
  4. 24-year-old man with narcolepsy on modafinil asks for a sleep aid: lies awake 2 hours most nights for a month sleep hygiene reviewed; no alcohol or opioids; no depression examination normal · urine drug screen negative → Suvorexant → suvorexant blocks orexin receptors, and narcolepsy can stem from orexin deficiency, so it is contraindicated; cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia comes first, and zolpidem acts at the benzodiazepine site
  5. 78-year-old woman with trouble falling asleep for 4 months sleeps through once asleep; cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia helped only partly uses a walker; one fall last year examination normal · no depression on screening → Ramelteon → ramelteon shortens time to sleep onset in older adults with a lower adverse-effect burden; antihistamines bring excessive sedation for little benefit, and benzodiazepines add dependence, confusion and falls
  6. 45-year-old man with generalized anxiety disorder, partly better after 10 weeks of sertraline alcohol use disorder, sober 1 year; drives a delivery truck wants an add-on that will not sedate him or become habit-forming examination normal → Add buspirone → buspirone, a partial agonist at serotonin 1A receptors, may be added when the response to an SSRI falls short and brings no sedation, tolerance or addiction; benzodiazepines carry risks of addiction and dependence, which he asked to avoid, and hydroxyzine is a sedating short-term add-on
  7. 39-year-old woman on clonazepam for panic disorder for 2 years, taken exactly as prescribed when a dose is late she feels shaky, sweaty and anxious no dose escalation, no early refills, no craving; working full time → Physiologic dependence → tolerance and withdrawal during supervised, prescribed use are expected physiology and do not count toward a use disorder, which needs problematic use with distress or impairment; a paradoxical reaction brings agitation and confusion, typically within an hour of a dose
  8. 52-year-old woman wakes at 3 AM most nights and cannot fall back asleep 4 months; sleep hygiene and cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia did not help no depression, snoring or alcohol; falls asleep easily examination normal → Eszopiclone → eszopiclone, like zolpidem, helps both falling and staying asleep and has the longest half-life of the Z-drugs; zaleplon and ramelteon help sleep onset only

Transferable rule

Name the half-life and the other depressants on board: a short half-life brings rebound and dependence, the liver favors a glucuronidated agent, and alcohol or an opioid turns sedation into respiratory depression.
